strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: active view selection for efficient 3D reconstruction, with relevance to robotics, digitization, and neural rendering.
Introduces a large-scale Neural Uncertainty Map (NUM) dataset of 62,400 viewpoint-UMap pairs across 13 ShapeNet categories, which could be useful for future work on learned view selection.

The proposed PUN/UPNet pipeline is simple and computationally efficient: it avoids retraining a neural rendering model during view selection and reports substantial speed and resource improvements over iterative NeRF-based baselines.
Evaluates with two different neural rendering backbones (NeRF and 3DGS), multiple image/mesh/coverage metrics, and both in-domain and out-of-domain object categories.
Includes useful ablations on uncertainty metrics, next-view selection policies, and training data composition.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: supervised prediction of next-best views or uncertainty from images has been explored before, and the core technical contribution is mainly a ViT regressor predicting a 48-dimensional uncertainty vector together with a heuristic aggregation/filtering policy.

The evaluation is restricted to synthetic, normalized, object-centric ShapeNet instances with fixed-radius spherical viewpoints. There is no real-world or large-scale scene evaluation, so practical applicability is unclear.

The claimed comparison to the “upper bound” is not convincing: the upper bound trains on the same 40 evaluation views used for testing, so it is an oracle rather than a fair held-out upper bound. The paper also claims “comparable” performance, but Table 1 shows clear gaps (e.g., in-domain PSNR 33.19 vs. 36.47; out-of-domain 34.74 vs. 36.91).

Baseline comparisons are incomplete: there is no random, uniform, coverage-greedy, or full-view training baseline, and improvements over the strongest AVS baseline are often small and may fall within the reported run-to-run variance. No statistical significance tests are provided.

The uncertainty maps are generated using SplatterImage and PSNR reconstruction errors, but the selected views are evaluated with NeRF and 3DGS. The mismatch between the uncertainty source and the downstream rendering model is not analyzed deeply, despite being central to the approach.

Some experimental reporting is inconsistent or unclear. For example, Table 4 reports PSNR around 37.4 while the main NeRF results in Table 1 report PSNR around 33.19, and it is not clearly specified which rendering model is used for the ablations.

The method assumes a fixed object-centric spherical camera setup, a known object center, fixed radius, and a single object per scene. This limits generalization to unconstrained 3D environments, as the authors acknowledge.

The dataset generation and UPNet training require a large amount of precomputed ground-truth uncertainty data derived from a specific single-view synthesis backbone, which may limit reproducibility and transfer to other sensing settings.

strengths: Introduces an amortized active view selection approach (PUN) that predicts neural uncertainty maps from a single view using a lightweight UPNet, avoiding per-step NeRF/3DGS retraining during inference.
Provides a large-scale synthetic NUM dataset with 62,400 viewpoint/UMap pairs across 13 ShapeNet categories, which may be useful for supervised uncertainty prediction research.
Evaluates the method with two downstream neural rendering models (NeRF and 3DGS) and includes in-domain and out-of-domain object category experiments.
Reports substantial inference-time compute and resource savings compared to iterative NeRF-based AVS baselines, with up to 400x speedup and reduced CPU/RAM/GPU usage.
Includes some useful ablations on uncertainty metrics, view-selection policies, and dataset diversity/density, and promises code, models, and datasets.
weaknesses: The central claim that PUN achieves reconstruction quality comparable to the all-views upper bound using only half the viewpoints is not supported by the reported results: gaps are substantial (e.g., ID PSNR 33.19 vs. 36.47; OOD PSNR 34.74 vs. 36.91), so 'on par' is overstated.

Evaluation is limited to synthetic ShapeNet objects with normalized, center-aligned geometry and spherical viewpoints; there is no real-world, large-scale, or arbitrary-viewpoint evaluation, limiting practical significance and generalizability claims.

Important baselines are missing, including random or coverage-based view selection, simple farthest-point/uniform sampling, information-gain heuristics, and recent 3DGS-based AVS methods (ActiveSplat, ActiveGS, ActiveGAMER) that are discussed but not compared.

Performance improvements over the strongest baseline (NVF) are often small relative to variance (e.g., ID PSNR 33.19±1.74 vs. NVF 33.08±0.44; OOD 34.74±2.81 vs. 33.15±2.42), and no statistical significance tests are provided.

There is a potential data leakage/confounding issue: ground-truth UMaps are generated using SplatterImage pretrained on ShapeNet, while evaluation is also on ShapeNet; it is unclear whether test instances or categories were seen during pretraining.

The uncertainty construction is unclear and possibly inconsistent: PSNR is a quality metric (higher is better) but is used as an 'uncertainty' measure; the threshold of 0.1 and aggregation product are not justified if raw PSNR values are used.

Technical details are insufficient for reproducibility: the ViT variant, interpolation angular units (degrees vs. radians), candidate sampling details, coordinate transformations, baseline hyperparameters, and dataset category list are missing or ambiguous.

Results appear inconsistent: Table 1 reports NeRF PSNR around 33.19, while Table 4 reports PSNR around 37.4 despite being described as NeRF-based, which is above the stated NeRF upper bound and suggests possible experimental mix-up.

The compute-efficiency comparison excludes UPNet training, NUM dataset generation, and pretraining costs, so the claimed 400x speedup reflects only inference and may not hold in total cost for smaller tasks.

Novelty is incremental: supervised prediction of next-best views or uncertainty from current observations has been explored; the main addition is amortized UMap prediction and aggregation, but the advantage over prior supervised/RL NBV methods is not clearly established.

Ablations show limited influence of key design choices (e.g., uncertainty metric choice is largely inconsequential), and the diversity/density results are weak, weakening the empirical case for the proposed components.

strengths: Introduces a novel and practical AVS formulation that predicts a neural uncertainty map directly from a single image, avoiding expensive iterative NeRF-based uncertainty computation and retraining during inference.
Contributes a large-scale NUM dataset with 62,400 viewpoint-UMap pairs across 13 ShapeNet categories and four uncertainty metrics, which is a useful resource for supervised active view selection.

Demonstrates substantial computational efficiency gains, reporting up to 400x speedup and over 50% reductions in CPU, RAM, and GPU usage during viewpoint selection compared with iterative AVS baselines.
Evaluates across in-domain and out-of-domain settings, multiple neural rendering backbones (NeRF and 3DGS), and diverse metrics covering image quality, mesh quality, and visual coverage.
Provides useful ablations on uncertainty metrics, redundancy filtering, aggregation policies, and dataset size/density trade-offs.
Shows promising generalization to novel object categories and rendering models without additional UPNet training, supporting the practical value of the approach.
The paper is clearly written, well illustrated, and promises code, models, and datasets, which supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: The claim that PUN achieves reconstruction accuracy 'comparable to the all-views upper bound' is overstated. In the in-domain NeRF setting, PSNR is 33.19 vs. 36.47 and MSE is 6.96 vs. 4.11; these are meaningful gaps, not simply comparable performance.

Improvements over the strongest baseline, NVF, are marginal in several important in-domain metrics and are often within reported standard deviations, weakening the central reconstruction-quality claim.

The evaluation omits recent AVS baselines such as ActiveSplat, ActiveGS, ActiveGAMER, and RL/supervised NBV methods, despite citing them; comparisons are limited to older NeRF-based baselines and an upper bound.

The setting is restricted to object-centric, centered ShapeNet objects with a fixed spherical viewpoint radius and known object center, limiting evidence for scaling to complex, large-scale, or unconstrained 3D scenes.

The candidate-viewpoint protocol may favor PUN: PUN samples 512 random candidates at each timestep and can select arbitrary viewpoints, while baselines use a fixed discrete candidate set, raising fairness concerns.

The reported 400x speedup and resource savings measure only the inference-time viewpoint selection phase and exclude the cost of NUM dataset generation and UPNet training, so total pipeline cost is not fully characterized.
Uncertainty maps are trained from image-level reconstruction errors of SplatterImage and may not reflect geometric uncertainty, which the authors acknowledge but do not fully resolve.
Out-of-domain evaluation uses only two unseen categories with 10 instances each, so the generalization claim to novel object categories is supported by a relatively narrow test set.

The method predicts uncertainty only at 48 fixed anchor points and relies on heuristic interpolation to arbitrary candidates; sensitivity to anchor resolution and interpolation strategy is not thoroughly analyzed.

strengths: Introduces a novel AVS framework, PUN, with UPNet predicting neural uncertainty maps from a single input image, avoiding expensive iterative retraining of neural rendering models during view selection.
Demonstrates substantial computational efficiency: up to 400x speedup and large reductions in CPU, RAM, GPU usage and GPU memory compared with NeRF-based AVS baselines.

Contributes the NUM dataset with 13 ShapeNet categories, 100 instances per category, 48 viewpoints per instance, and uncertainty maps under four metrics, which is a useful resource for active view selection research.

Provides extensive experiments across novel instances, novel categories, different reconstruction backbones (NeRF, 3DGS, Binocular3DGS), lighting changes, camera distance changes, NeRFAssets, and MIP360, plus multiple ablations.

Shows generalization to unseen object categories and to different downstream reconstruction backbones without retraining, and offers interpretable UMap visualizations with reported correlation to ground-truth uncertainty.
The paper is generally well organized and clearly explains the overall AVS pipeline, dataset generation, selection policies, and ablation studies.
weaknesses: The central assumption—that uncertainty maps derived from single-view 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstruction error transfer effectively to multi-view NeRF/3DGS active view selection—is not fully theoretically or empirically validated; the PUN-NeRF variant is tested only on a small airplane subset, and the correlation analysis with view-complexity metrics is indirect.

Missing comparisons with recent state-of-the-art AVS methods such as ActiveSplat, ActiveGS, and ActiveGAMER, which are cited but not used as baselines. The main tables also omit some baselines such as WD and Uniform for several settings, making the empirical comparison incomplete.

On some key benchmarks, improvements are marginal and may not be statistically significant, e.g., NUM-inst PSNR 33.19 vs. NVF 33.08, with large standard deviations in the supplement; the paper often reports average results in the main text without uncertainty estimates.

Real-world evaluation is limited: MIP360 uses only four object-centric scenes with low absolute PSNR (17.49), and the method assumes spherical, fixed-radius, object-centered viewpoints, which restricts claims about unconstrained 3D environments.

The uncertainty map is a 48-dimensional anchor vector with simple softmax interpolation and heuristic product aggregation; there is limited justification that this approximates principled information gain or true radiance-field uncertainty.

The NUM dataset and UPNet rely on ShapeNet and SplatterImage, which may limit transferability to truly novel domains or categories outside the synthetic training distribution; the MIP360 protocol also retains only centered-object views and may not reflect general active reconstruction.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: active view selection for efficient neural 3D reconstruction, with clear practical motivation.
Introduces UPNet, a lightweight feedforward uncertainty-map predictor that avoids retraining a neural rendering model after each selected view, enabling large runtime and resource savings.
Contributes a sizeable NUM dataset with 62,400 viewpoint-UMap pairs across 13 ShapeNet categories and four uncertainty metrics; this could be a useful resource if properly released.

Provides extensive experiments across multiple datasets, reconstruction backbones, lighting/camera variations, and ablations, with consistently strong empirical results against the included baselines.
Demonstrates substantial computational efficiency gains, including faster view selection and lower CPU/GPU/RAM usage, which is a meaningful practical advantage.
weaknesses: Critical evaluation flaw: the reported Upper-bnd trains on the same evaluation views used for novel-view synthesis. This makes it an oracle/memorization baseline rather than an upper bound for novel-view synthesis, so the central claim that PUN matches the upper bound using half the views is unsupported and misleading.

Uncertainty construction and scaling are unclear and likely inconsistent. PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS/MSE are not directly uncertainty values, but the paper does not explain normalization, inversion, or how thresholds such as 0.1 and product aggregation operate. This harms reproducibility and technical clarity.

Missing comparisons to recent and directly relevant AVS methods cited in the paper, such as ActiveSplat, ActiveGS, ActiveGAMER, Smith et al. 2022, and Neu-NBV. The empirical positioning against current SOTA is therefore incomplete.

Real-world generalization evidence is weak. On MIP360, reported SSIM is only around 0.29 and experiments cover just four scenes; mesh completion ratios are also low (~0.18), so geometry-aware reconstruction claims are not convincingly supported.

The core proxy assumption is not sufficiently justified: single-view SplatterImage reconstruction error is used as a surrogate for multi-view NeRF/3DGS uncertainty. The paper offers only moderate correlations with handcrafted complexity measures, not a rigorous validation across occlusion, background clutter, or different view-selection regimes.

Reproducibility is compromised: the manuscript states that code, models, and datasets are available at a URL, but no actual link appears. Several implementation details for UPNet training, UMap normalization, interpolation at poles, and candidate-view handling are missing.

Some claims are overstated. For example, it is claimed that PUN outperforms all baselines on all eight metrics, but Uniform is competitive or tied on visual coverage in the supplement. The 400x speedup claim also relies on resource comparisons that are not fully apples-to-apples across methods.

There are minor inconsistencies and typos, e.g., anchor-number ablation entries appear as 89 instead of 48 in the main table, and some reported CPU/resource numbers differ between text and supplement. These reduce confidence in the experimental reporting.

strengths: Introduces PUN, a novel AVS pipeline that predicts neural uncertainty maps directly from a single image via a lightweight ViT-based UPNet, avoiding costly retraining of neural rendering models during view selection.
Achieves substantial computational efficiency: up to ~350-400x faster view selection and >50% reductions in CPU, RAM, and GPU usage compared to NeRF-based AVS baselines.
Contributes a large-scale NUM dataset (62,400 viewpoint-UMap pairs across 13 ShapeNet categories), which is a useful resource for supervised uncertainty prediction and active view selection.

Extensive evaluation spans multiple datasets (NUM-inst, NUM-cat, NUM-light, NUM-cam-dist, NeRFAssets, MIP360), three reconstruction backbones (NeRF, 3DGS, Binocular3DGS), and multiple image/mesh/coverage metrics.
Demonstrates generalization to unseen object categories, lighting changes, camera distance changes, and realistic scenes without additional training or fine-tuning.

Provides interpretable uncertainty maps with a reported 0.82 Pearson correlation to ground-truth UMaps, plus ablations on uncertainty metrics, selection policies, dataset size, anchor number, and redundancy threshold.
weaknesses: The central claim of achieving reconstruction quality 'comparable' to the upper bound with half the views is overstated. For example, on NUM-inst PSNR is 33.19 vs. 36.47 and MSE is 6.96 vs. 4.11; on NUM-cat PSNR is 34.74 vs. 36.91, which are meaningful gaps rather than near-parity.

The upper-bound protocol trains on the same 40 evaluation views used for testing, making it an oracle that has already seen the test views. This is not directly comparable to AVS methods that select 20 training views and are evaluated on held-out novel views, weakening the upper-bound comparison.

Missing comparisons to recent/3DGS-based AVS methods such as ActiveSplat, ActiveGS, ActiveGAMER, and learning-based NBV methods like RL-NBV or supervised NBV, despite discussing them. The empirical comparison relies mainly on older NeRF uncertainty baselines (WD, A-NeRF, NVF) and Uniform.

The UMap supervision is derived from single-view SplatterImage reconstructions and PSNR errors at 48 fixed anchors. This is a heuristic proxy for uncertainty and may not fully capture multi-view geometric uncertainty or downstream NeRF/3DGS reconstruction difficulty.
Reproducibility is only partially supported: code, models, and datasets are claimed to be available, but the provided manuscript lacks the actual URL/link.

The method assumes object-centric spherical viewpoint distributions with a fixed radius and center-aligned objects; real-world unconstrained 3D environments may violate these assumptions, limiting the generality of the MIP360/NeRFAssets claims.

Improvements over the strongest NeRF-based baseline (NVF) are small on same-category instances (e.g., +0.11 dB PSNR on NUM-inst), though gains are larger on novel categories, 3DGS reconstruction, and some environment shifts.
